Constraint Handling Rules, a rule-based programming language, has been extensively utilized in bioinformatics for modeling and simulating biological systems. Despite its widespread application, a comprehensive understanding of its capabilities remains limited. This paper delves into the theoretical underpinnings of Constraint Handling Rules by examining its expressive power. We establish that Constraint Handling Rules is Turing complete when rule heads consist of more than one atom, and demonstrate its limitations when the heads consist of a single atom. We also establish a polynomial time complexity for Constraint Handling Rules and provide a linear time solution for a restricted version of the language.

We investigate the relationship between galaxy spin and large-scale structure in the SDSS DR7, DR12, and 2MASS Redshift Survey, focusing on the alignment of these axes. Our analysis reveals that the dipole in galaxy spin alignment is consistent across surveys, with the spin axes pointing towards the same direction. Furthermore, we observe that the spin alignment follows a consistent pattern with the matter dipole and galaxy distribution dipole, with the strength of this alignment increasing with distance from the observer. Our findings also indicate that the spin alignment is influenced by the large-scale structure of the universe, with the strength of this influence varying depending on the distance from the observer.

We introduce a novel approach called Eigen-Reptile, a meta-learning algorithm that
effectively addresses the challenges of few-shot learning, including sampling bias
and noisy labels. This method integrates the strengths of Reptile, a continuous
meta-learning method, with the eigenspace of the covariance matrix of the meta-batch,
allowing for more stable and efficient learning. By doing so, Eigen-Reptile achieves
better performance on standard few-shot benchmarks, such as miniImageNet, and
outperforms existing methods in handling noisy labels, as demonstrated by our
experiments on the noisy miniImageNet dataset.

Alzheimer's disease is a widespread neurodegenerative disorder that significantly affects the elderly population. Researchers are actively working to develop predictive models for the disease, which can help identify individuals at risk and inform early intervention strategies. This study presents a novel approach to predicting the Mini-PET score, a key indicator of cognitive function, using a deep learning model that incorporates both MRI and PET data. Our model, which combines a 3D convolutional neural network and a graph convolutional neural network, outperforms existing methods in predicting the Mini-PET score, achieving a high correlation of 0.81. These findings demonstrate the potential of our model to improve Alzheimer's disease prediction and diagnosis.

The field of AI Ethics is rapidly growing, with numerous frameworks and initiatives emerging. This article examines the ethical implications of AI initiatives, focusing on their alignment with recent advancements in AI Ethics research. It assesses 100 AI initiatives, highlighting their emphasis on social responsibility and human-centric values. The analysis reveals a need for a more nuanced ethical evaluation, prompting a call for AI initiatives to integrate moral considerations into their design and development processes.

We investigate the properties of the language classes compatible with the Boolean operations over infinite words, specifically within the context of the $\omega$-words. We demonstrate that the only language class that is decidable, Boolean-closed, and fulfills the full trio criteria over $\omega$-words is the class of the regular languages. This outcome is achieved by proving a theorem stating that any Boolean-closed full trio over $\omega$-words must be capable of recognizing the language consisting of all $\omega$-words.

This research introduces a hybrid channel estimation technique that combines the benefits of both pilot-based and compressed sensing methods. It utilizes a deep neural network to model the channel's time-frequency characteristics, thereby reducing the need for extensive pilot data. The proposed approach is then integrated with orthogonal matching pursuit to achieve channel estimation. The results demonstrate that the hybrid method offers superior accuracy and reduced complexity compared to existing techniques.

Recent anomalies in the values of V_{ud} and V_{us} have the potential to provide
new insights into physics beyond the Standard Model, as they are influenced by
multiple factors. This work examines the implications of these anomalies within
the context of a specific model that incorporates a light scalar and a new
charged fermion. We explore how the new physics parameters can be constrained
by existing experimental data and discuss the potential for future measurements
to further refine our understanding of these phenomena.

This research introduces a novel approach to designing convolutional layers that utilize dilated kernels, enabling the incorporation of diverse receptive fields within a single layer. By integrating this concept into the ResNet-50 framework, we developed a dilated network that outperforms its original counterpart in image classification, object detection, and segmentation tasks. Furthermore, we observed that the dilated network's efficiency can be further enhanced by selectively removing kernels with minimal impact on performance.

In the context of data analysis, we consider a scenario where a server possesses a dataset consisting of numerous data views, with each view containing a subset of attributes. The individual and overlapping information between these views is safeguarded by separate encryption keys held by different parties. The server, which holds the combined data, is unable to access the private data without the unique key. The objective is to enable the server to perform computations on the data views while maintaining confidentiality. We present a solution that utilizes the algebraic properties of encrypted data to facilitate data aggregation, thereby ensuring privacy preservation. The proposed method is demonstrated through its application to real-world data sets, including the 2016 US Census data and the 2016 US Election data.

We have conducted a study on the hot dust emission in a large sample of galaxies, analyzing 10,000 galaxies from the WISE and Spitzer surveys. By comparing the infrared data with radio observations from the LOFAR survey, we found that the hot dust emission is a significant factor in the infrared emission of galaxies, particularly in those with high infrared luminosity. We found that the hot dust emission is more prevalent in galaxies with high infrared luminosity and that the contribution of hot dust emission increases with the mass of the galaxy. We also found that the hot dust emission is more prevalent in galaxies with a smooth structure and that the contribution of star formation to the infrared emission is lower in galaxies with a high mass. These findings suggest that the hot dust emission is a significant factor in the infrared emission of galaxies, particularly in galaxies with high mass and a smooth structure.

To develop AI systems that can reason morally like humans, it's crucial to understand human moral judgment. This study explores the effectiveness of prompting large language models to simulate moral reasoning, using a method called MORALCOT. By having the model generate and refine moral reasoning in a step-by-step process, it can improve its performance on moral judgment tasks. The results show that MORALCOT significantly enhances AI systems' ability to make moral judgments, particularly when combined with a strong language model. The method also allows for the creation of AI systems that can perform well on various moral judgment tasks, including those that require nuanced understanding of human values and moral reasoning.
We demonstrate that a valuation ring with a residue field of characteristic p can be expressed as a direct sum of algebras over fields with p^r elements, where r ranges from 1 to infinity.

This paper explores the concept of two-dimensional Dirac equation in the context of a curved spacetime, specifically within the framework of Einstein-Cartan theory. We delve into its applications in various physical systems, including graphene, quantum wells, and axion electrodynamics, and examine the behavior of spin connection coefficients in these environments.

Cooperative driving applications are increasingly reliant on Model Predictive Control (MPC) for enhanced performance. However, MPC's computational complexity poses a significant challenge, particularly in applications requiring real-time operation. To address this issue, a new approach is proposed, which involves approximating the optimal solution to a quadratic program (QP) within a MPC framework. This method leverages a neural network to predict the optimal control input, thereby significantly reducing computation time. The proposed method's efficacy is demonstrated through a numerical example, which showcases its ability to achieve real-time operation while maintaining performance comparable to an MPC-QP approach.

In recent years, the proliferation of social media platforms has led to a significant increase in the spread of misinformation, which has been linked to the erosion of trust in information credibility. This erosion of trust has been exacerbated by the ease of sharing unverified information on these platforms. To address this issue, researchers have been exploring the use of machine learning techniques to identify and mitigate the spread of misinformation. This study focuses on the development of a machine learning model that can effectively detect fake news on social media platforms. By analyzing a dataset of fake news articles, the researchers were able to develop a model that achieved a high level of accuracy in identifying fake news. The results of this study demonstrate the potential of machine learning techniques to address the issue of misinformation on social media platforms.

In the context of vehicular networks, the integration of vehicular ad-hoc networks (VANETs) and cellular networks is becoming increasingly important. However, the complex nature of this integration poses significant challenges, particularly in terms of network management and resource allocation. To address these issues, we propose a novel framework called $\pi$-ROAD, which leverages the capabilities of both network types to provide seamless connectivity and efficient resource allocation. The key innovation of $\pi$-ROAD lies in its ability to dynamically allocate resources based on the specific needs of each vehicle, while also taking into account the unique characteristics of both network types. To validate the effectiveness of $\pi$-ROAD, we conducted extensive simulations using real-world data and compared the results with those of existing approaches. The results demonstrate that $\pi$-ROAD outperforms its counterparts in terms of network performance, resource utilization, and energy efficiency. The results also highlight the importance of considering the specific needs of each vehicle when designing network management systems. Overall, $\pi$-ROAD represents a significant step forward in the integration of VANETs and cellular networks, and has the potential to revolutionize the way we manage and manage network resources during emergencies.

This research introduces a novel approach to enhance the path of a robot-assisted collaborative task by integrating an Artificial Potential Fields collision avoidance system. The study focuses on a collaborative task where a robot and a human work together to place a part onto a larger assembly. The robot's path is optimized by avoiding collisions with obstacles and ensuring the human's safety through the APF method. The study compares the enhanced path with the original path and evaluates the impact of the human's involvement on the task's completion time. The results demonstrate that the APF method successfully avoids collisions and ensures the human's safety without impeding the task's efficiency.

The rise of autonomous vehicles and smart devices in our daily lives is transforming the urban landscape, necessitating a shift towards cities that accommodate autonomous systems. This shift is reflected in the evolving dynamics of urban mobility, where vehicles and pedestrians coexist, and the need for intelligent infrastructure is becoming increasingly apparent. To facilitate this transition, cities must be reimagined to accommodate the complex interactions between autonomous systems and the surrounding environment. This is where the concept of a digital twin comes into play, offering a virtual representation of the physical world that can be leveraged to optimize urban mobility. This paper explores the potential of digital twins in enhancing urban mobility, highlighting their benefits and the challenges that need to be addressed to fully realize their benefits.

In the context of online caching, we've developed a new approach that leverages predictive analytics to enhance performance. This innovative method incorporates a prediction model that forecasts future requests, and uses these forecasts to determine the optimal cache configuration. Our analysis reveals that the effectiveness of this approach depends on the accuracy of the prediction model and the size of the cache. Specifically, we've found that a competitive ratio of $O(\sqrt{m})$ can be achieved, where $m$ represents the maximum prediction error. Furthermore, we've demonstrated that a competitive ratio of $O(m)$ can be attained, and we've also explored the limitations of this approach, showing that a ratio of $O(\log m)$ is unattainable.

A novel neural network architecture, the Trilateral Attention Network (TAN), has been developed for the task of image segmentation. This model incorporates three distinct pathways, each with unique attention mechanisms, to capture different types of contextual information. The first pathway, focusing on local relationships, is enhanced by a self-attention module, while the second leverages non-local block interactions through a non-local attention module. The third pathway, combining spatial and channel attention, is achieved through a dual-attention module. The three pathways are integrated through a fusion module, which is trainable and allows for the network to learn the optimal fusion strategy. Experimental results on the PASCAL VOC 2012 and Cityscapes datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the TAN model, outperforming other state-of-the-art methods.

In this context, the torsion constraints are formulated in terms of the gauge fields and their derivatives, and we demonstrate that these fields can be eliminated to obtain a simplified, torsion-free covariant derivative.

The quality of training data is a crucial factor in determining the effectiveness of learning models. To address this issue, we've developed a method that leverages the predictive performance of models trained on specific data subsets to evaluate the quality of individual data examples. By analyzing how models perform when trained on data without a particular example, we can determine whether that example is beneficial or detrimental to the model. This approach is grounded in the concept of negative data, which refers to data examples that negatively impact a model's performance. By quantifying the contribution of positive and negative data examples to a model's performance, we can identify the most valuable data for training. We've tested this method on various datasets, including image and text data, and found that it effectively identifies high-quality data examples. Furthermore, we've discovered that our method can be used to identify the most valuable data for training, and that it can be used to identify the most valuable data for training a model on a specific task.

We introduce METRO-LM, a series of 500M-1.5B parameter language models, which are designed to be efficient yet highly effective. These models demonstrate competitive performance on various benchmarks, including MMLU, FActS, and others, while being 2-4 times smaller than their counterparts. METRO-LM models are trained using a unique approach that combines a large-scale pre-training dataset with a smaller, high-quality pre-training dataset, resulting in improved performance. We also release METRO-LM models in 256, 512, and 768 dimension variants, which are available for public use.

Introducing visual representations to the audience is a crucial step in the visualization process, yet the lack of a standardized approach makes it challenging to determine the most effective method. To address this issue, we conducted a study to compare the performance of text-based and non-text-based introductions, using a case study involving a visualization that compares the performance of different machine learning models. Our research involved testing various introduction methods, including non-textual, text-based, and interactive introductions, and evaluating their effectiveness through user studies. Our results show that text-based introductions are the most effective, particularly when they include a description of the visualization's purpose and a brief explanation of the data being presented. Furthermore, we found that interactive introductions can be effective in certain contexts, but they are not always necessary. Our research provides valuable insights into the design of visualizations and can help designers create more effective introductions for their audiences.

The optical manipulation of many-body systems is a cutting-edge research area in quantum physics.  By rapidly switching on and off a laser, researchers can create artificial periodic forces that can be used to control the behavior of these systems.  However, the laser's periodic nature can also lead to unwanted heating of the system, which can destroy its ordered state.  In this study, we investigate how the system's order is affected by the rate of this heating, and find that it can be controlled by adjusting the frequency and amplitude of the laser.  Our research shows that the system's order can be preserved even when it is subjected to rapid changes, and that it can be used to create new types of quantum materials.  These findings open up new possibilities for the study of quantum systems and the development of new materials with exotic properties.

Counterfactual planning is a method that utilizes past experiences to create innovative plans, but its effectiveness is hindered by the assumption that the model parameters are accurate. In reality, model parameters are often uncertain, leading to the possibility that plans generated using counterfactual planning may not be reliable. To investigate this issue, we conducted a simulation study using a complex model of the US economy and found that plans created using counterfactual planning are less effective when the model parameters are uncertain. To mitigate this problem, we developed a new approach that incorporates the uncertainty of model parameters into the planning process. Our method involves using a Bayesian inference technique to estimate the model parameters and then using these estimates to create more robust plans. We tested our approach using a real-world scenario and found that it produces more effective plans than traditional counterfactual planning.

This research presents a novel approach to classifying urban sounds using a combination of convolutional neural networks and attention mechanisms. The model is trained on a large dataset of 10,000 10-second audio clips, each annotated with one of 20 distinct sound categories. The proposed method is evaluated on two benchmark datasets, achieving state-of-the-art results with accuracy rates of 90.5% and 89.7% on the ESC-50 and US8k datasets, respectively. The model's performance is further demonstrated through a detailed analysis of its predictions on the DCAS2 dataset.

Cain is a high-level programming language that compiles efficiently into machine code for the SCAMP-5 chip, surpassing the performance of other compilers. The language's syntax is intuitive, facilitating the creation of code for the SCAMP-5 chip, and the code produced by Cain is compact, efficient, and easy to read, with a smaller size compared to code produced by the C compiler for the SCAMP-5 chip.

A recent study by Letcher et al. (2022) proposed a pioneering method for learning mixed-strategy Nash equilibria through a combination of multi-agent reinforcement learning and best response computation. This method employs a process known as regret pruning to iteratively remove actions that are suboptimal, ultimately converging to a mixed-strategy equilibrium. However, regret pruning can be computationally expensive, limiting its application to games with a small number of actions. To address this limitation, we have developed two new regret pruning variations that utilize the concept of regret minimization to improve upon the original approach. Specifically, we have introduced two variations: one that prunes actions with a low regret value, and another that prunes actions with a high regret value. We have demonstrated that these variations can achieve better performance than the original regret pruning method in a variety of games, including the Prisoner's Dilemma and the Matching Pennies game. Furthermore, we have shown that these variations can be used to learn Nash equilibria in games with a large number of actions, such as the Rock-Paper-Scissors game. Overall, our results demonstrate the potential of regret pruning as a tool for learning mixed-strategy equilibria in complex games.

We've developed a new modal logic that builds on existing work by Kanger and Lemmon, incorporating their ideas on modal and predicate logic. This logic is represented by a specific system, including a key axiom, and we've established its fundamental properties. Furthermore, we've applied this logic to enhance Aristotle's modal syllogistic framework, expanding its scope to encompass more complex state-of-affairs propositions.

We introduce a method to reduce the efficiency needed for violating quantum and classical causal inequalities. By linking these inequalities to Bell inequalities, we find that quantum and classical causal inequalities can be violated at 100% efficiency. Our technique can be applied universally, allowing for the creation of new causal inequalities that are less reliant on efficiency.

This study introduces an innovative dual-critic reinforcement learning framework for optimizing video encoding. The proposed method leverages two separate reward signals to concurrently address the challenges of minimizing distortion and adhering to a rate limit. By employing two distinct policy gradient estimators, our framework effectively resolves the trade-off between these competing objectives. The proposed framework is evaluated using the OpenLM rate control model and outperforms the existing state-of-the-art method on multiple metrics, including PSNR, SSIM, and VMAF.

Recent research has shown that the gas-phase chemistry in protoplanetary disks is heavily influenced by the movement of carbon-rich grains. These grains can be broken down into smaller particles by a process called photo-ablation, releasing carbon into the gas phase. This process can be sustained over long periods, as it is not affected by the depletion of carbon in the gas phase. This is because the newly released carbon can form complex molecules, which can then be converted into more complex forms, such as carbon monoxide. This cycle can be maintained even in the presence of carbon monoxide, which is a common component of these disks. This research has also found that the movement of carbon in these disks can be influenced by the presence of carbon monoxide, which can be a key factor in understanding the formation of complex molecules in these disks.

In solving complex mixed-integer linear programs (MILPs), cutting plane techniques are crucial for narrowing down the solution space. However, choosing the most suitable cuts for these problems is a challenging task. To address this issue, we present a novel neural network-based model, NeuralCut, designed to efficiently select cuts for MIP solvers. By training NeuralCut on a vast dataset of 10 million cuttings, we demonstrate its ability to outperform existing baseline models and achieve significant improvements in solving MILPs. Notably, NeuralCut's performance is particularly impressive when dealing with large-scale industrial problems, where it achieves a 10% to 20% reduction in solving time.

Bug reporting systems are crucial for software development, allowing developers to identify and fix defects efficiently. However, the sheer volume of bug reports can overwhelm developers, making it essential to streamline the reporting process. This study focuses on enhancing bug report retrieval by identifying identical and similar bug reports, thereby improving search efficiency. A novel NLP-based approach is proposed to retrieve identical bug reports, while a hybrid method is developed to retrieve similar bug reports, integrating the NLP-based approach. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of these methods in retrieving highly relevant bug reports, with the NLP-based approach achieving a 90% retrieval rate and the hybrid approach achieving a 95% retrieval rate.

We investigate the effective field theory of graphene near its critical point, where it exhibits universal behavior. This theory is characterized by a strongly coupled nature, which can be analyzed using the epsilon expansion method. By employing the conformal bootstrap technique, we establish rigorous bounds on the theory's parameters, specifically the anomalous dimension and its derivative. These constraints are derived from the properties of the four-point function of the stress-energy tensor and the implications of the $c$-theorem. Notably, we find that the conformal bootstrap approach yields tighter bounds on the anomalous dimension than the epsilon expansion, particularly in relation to the $c$-theorem.

This study introduces an innovative self-training framework that leverages a teacher-student approach to enhance Named Entity Recognition (NER) models. The framework incorporates a novel method for generating pseudo labels, which are then used to train a student model and refine its performance. We have thoroughly evaluated the framework's effectiveness on various NER datasets, including the CoNLL-2003 dataset, and found that it significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, including BERT-based models, by a substantial margin. The proposed framework's success is attributed to its ability to effectively utilize pseudo labels and its ability to adapt to different datasets. The framework's performance is particularly noteworthy in its ability to achieve high F1 scores on the OntoNotes 5.0 dataset, which is a challenging dataset for NER models. Overall, our results demonstrate the potential of the proposed framework to improve the performance of NER models on a wide range of datasets.

The analysis of social media data, such as tweets, can provide valuable insights for businesses and organizations in the tourism industry. By understanding user behavior and preferences, companies can make informed decisions about their products and services. This research presents a novel approach to analyzing tourism-related tweets using a combination of topic modeling and a neural network-based classifier. The methodology involves identifying key topics, classifying user preferences, and predicting future behavior based on the analysis of social media data. The study's findings demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in providing actionable insights for businesses and organizations in the tourism industry.

This study employs a machine learning approach to predict the effective properties of microstructured materials based on their microstructure. The proposed method involves training a neural network on a dataset of finite element simulations, where the network takes a microstructure image as input and outputs the effective property. The network is then used to predict the effective properties of various microstructured materials, including those with different geometries and material properties. The study demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach by comparing its predictions to those obtained from a more computationally expensive finite element simulation. The results show that the neural network can accurately predict the effective properties of microstructured materials, even when the input images are noisy or corrupted. The study also investigates the effect of different neural network architectures on the accuracy of predictions, and finds that a simple convolutional neural network can achieve high accuracy with a relatively small dataset. Overall, this study demonstrates the potential of machine learning to predict the effective properties of microstructured materials, and provides a framework for applying this approach to a wide range of materials and geometries.

The presence of a non-trivial solution is investigated for a non-local operator of an integro-differential type, influenced by the fractional gradient of order s, within the N-Torino space, where N is at least 2, and s falls within the range (N/2, 1). The study is based on the concept of "small data," which is a notion introduced by the authors in their 2019 publication.

This research focuses on multi-object filtering in unlabelled environments, specifically addressing trajectory estimation. We introduce a novel method that leverages a variational Bayesian framework to derive a closed-form solution for the Gaussian mixture model, enabling more accurate trajectory estimation. This approach is compatible with existing multi-object filtering methods, such as the Multi-Bernoulli Mixtures (MBM) and the Multi-Bernoulli Poisson Gibbs (MBM-PG) filter, and can be seamlessly integrated. We demonstrate the efficacy of this method through simulations involving both artificial and real-world scenarios.

The integration of power converters into the power grid has significantly altered the dynamic characteristics of the system, making traditional stability assessment methods inadequate. To address this issue, a novel approach is proposed, which assesses the stability of large power grids by analyzing the stability of its constituent subsystems. This method is based on the premise that the stability of a subsystem can be determined by analyzing the stability of its individual components. The proposed approach is demonstrated to be effective in assessing the stability of large power grids with high-penetration of power converters. The proposed approach is applied to a 100-bus power grid with high-penetration of power converters, and the results show that the proposed approach is more accurate than traditional methods. The proposed approach is also shown to be more efficient than traditional methods in terms of computational complexity.

The verification of a person's identity through signature validation is a crucial aspect of numerous applications, including legal and financial transactions. However, the variability of a person's signature can make it challenging to create a reliable validation system. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach to forgery detection that takes into account the unique characteristics of a person's signature, including its distinctiveness, complexity, and repeatability. By analyzing the signature's dynamic features, we can identify the most relevant information for validating the signature. Our method involves using a deep learning approach to extract these features and train a model to recognize valid signatures. Our experiments on multiple datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, which outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and robustness.

Mobile app developers can significantly enhance personalization by leveraging context, which refers to the current state of the mobile device and user. This allows for customized apps that adapt to users' immediate needs and location. However, accessing and utilizing context can be challenging, as it requires constant updates and can be resource-intensive. To address this issue, we introduce a context caching system that minimizes unnecessary context queries by storing and persisting relevant data. Our approach, which is integrated into the Android framework, reduces unnecessary context queries by 90% and decreases the associated energy consumption by 18%.

This research presents a groundbreaking approach to pose estimation, which can be executed in real-time on a standard laptop. Our method leverages a compact, efficient network that produces a single output image, which is then processed by a lightweight decoder to generate the 3D pose. By utilizing a pre-trained image encoder, we can achieve exceptional performance with minimal additional training, which is accomplished using a dataset of 3D models rendered in the target style. Our method, which is applicable to various image styles, is demonstrated through successful results on a dataset of 3D models rendered in the style of a cartoon character.

This device is capable of measuring the energy spectrum of X-ray sources in the 2-10 keV range with exceptional precision. This paper introduces a classification system for blockchain protocols based on their permission structure. We categorize a protocol as either "permissionless" or "permissioned" according to the level of control over node creation and transaction submission. Our analysis reveals that existing blockchain protocols can be classified into one of these two categories. Furthermore, we identify key characteristics of permissionless protocols, which can inform the design of new protocols, and highlight the potential for hybrid systems that combine the benefits of both models.

A new model for the interaction between chromoelectric dipoles in tetraquark states has been proposed, which takes into account the effects of confinement and the exchange of gluons. This model has been used to calculate the masses of several tetraquark states, including those with different quark compositions and quantum numbers. The results of this model are in good agreement with experimental data for a number of states, including the X(3872), Z_c(3900), and Z_c(4020). The improved model also provides a good description of the mass spectra of several other tetraquark states, including the Z_c(4020) and X(4272). The improved model is able to account for the effects of both the exchange of gluons and the confinement of quarks, which is essential for a complete understanding of the masses of tetraquark states.

In a modified version of the Standard Model, we've examined the implications of introducing a new scalar field that interacts with the Higgs boson, particularly focusing on the constraints imposed by the Higgs mass in such extensions. We've found that the presence of a new scalar field can lead to the breakdown of the Higgs potential at high energy scales, thereby limiting the Higgs mass. We've identified a specific type of interaction that can result in the breakdown of the Higgs potential at a scale of approximately 1000 GeV, thereby imposing a limit on the Higgs mass. We've also discovered that the presence of a new scalar field can lead to the breakdown of the Higgs mass limit, thereby allowing for a wider range of Higgs masses. This research focuses on the relationship between the HJ equation and the p-Talagrand inequality in Carnot groups, with a specific emphasis on how the HJ equation's weak solutions can be used to derive optimal logarithmic Sobolev and Talagrand inequalities. The study also presents novel logarithmic Sobolev and p-Talagrand inequalities in various settings, including He-type Finsler sub-Riemannian spaces, oriented Finsler sub-Riemannian spaces, and a specific class of Finsler Lie groups.

This research introduces a novel estimator called the exponentially weighted divergence estimator, built upon the density power divergence estimator. It is demonstrated that the proposed estimator surpasses the traditional density power divergence estimator in terms of robustness and efficiency. Furthermore, it is shown that the exponentially weighted divergence estimator retains the same asymptotic properties as the density power divergence estimator. To validate its performance, a simulation study and a real data analysis were conducted.

This paper introduces a new method for generating a static scene representation from a single image, drawing inspiration from the concept of a static camera. The proposed algorithm uses a pixel-wise approach to identify the static scene, leveraging the interdependence of pixels to distinguish between static and motion-centric pixels. The algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated through its application to multi-focus images, where it identifies regions of interest and facilitates the creation of sharp images. The algorithm's performance is evaluated using multi-focus images, where it successfully identifies regions of interest and produces sharp images.

The characteristic polynomial of a random $d$-regular graph, denoted as $X_d$, is a well-studied object in mathematics.  The coefficients of this polynomial are random variables whose statistical properties are of interest.  The variance of the constant term in the polynomial is known to be $\frac{1}{2}d^2 + O(1)$, whereas the variance of the linear coefficient is $\frac{1}{3}d^2 + O(1)$.  The purpose of this research is to establish a general formula for the variance of the $k$-th coefficient of $X_d$, and to demonstrate that the leading term in this formula is $k^{2}d^2 + O(d^k)$.  The research reveals that the leading term in the formula is driven by the number of self-intersecting periodic orbits in the graph, and that the variance of the linear coefficient is unique in its behavior.  The research also shows that the variance of the $k$-th coefficient of $X_d$ is concentrated in a particular range of values, and that the probability of the $k$-th coefficient exceeding this range is exponentially small.  The research also provides a general formula for the variance of the $k$-th coefficient of $X_d$, and that the formula is valid for all values of $k$.

This research investigates the properties of negative and positive imaginary systems, which are essential in the study of H-infinity stability. We examine the ways in which negative imaginary systems can be derived from positive imaginary systems through system transformations, and we establish a method for identifying a nearest negative imaginary system for any given linear time-invariant system. We also explore the properties of the set of all possible negative imaginary systems for linear time-invariant and dynamic systems, and we establish a method for identifying a minimal-norm element within this set.

This study investigates the effectiveness of continual learning in End-to-End Automatic Speech Recognition. We introduce a new baseline model that utilizes a variational inference approach to enhance the representation of speech data. We also present a new method for continual learning that builds upon this baseline. Our experiments, conducted on the Librispeech dataset, demonstrate that the state-of-the-art continual learning technique surpasses the performance of fine-tuning by 0.5% in terms of Word Error Rate. Furthermore, we introduce a new method for assessing the performance of continual learning algorithms, which measures the rate of improvement in Word Error Rate as more tasks are added. Our results show that the proposed method achieves a 10% improvement in this metric compared to the current best continual learning technique.

The widespread use of social media has led to the emergence of code-switching, a phenomenon where individuals combine multiple languages within a single message. This language mixing has significant implications for sentiment analysis, as the meaning of a message can change drastically depending on the languages used. To address this issue, we have developed a new approach to sentiment analysis that leverages multilingual word embeddings to handle code-switching. Our method involves training a neural network that can switch between different languages based on the context, and we have evaluated its performance on a dataset of Indonesian-Malaysian code-switching messages. The results show that our approach outperforms existing methods, achieving a 2.5% increase in accuracy.

A recent study revealed that a specific type of particle, known as a triplet fermion, is a viable candidate for explaining the small masses of neutrinos. This particle, which is a key component of the three-loop seesaw model, has been constrained by the LHC's search for top quark partners. We have conducted an in-depth analysis of the three-loop seesaw model, taking into account the constraints from neutrino mass and mixing, as well as the LHC's search for top quark partners. Our findings indicate that the mass of the triplet fermion must be less than 129 GeV at a 95% confidence level, assuming the Higgs boson mass is 125 GeV.

This paper introduces a novel method for Neural Network (NN) based feature transformation, which is designed to enhance the performance of Product Neural Network (PNN) models in handling categorical data. The PNN model utilizes a product layer to capture interactions between categorical fields, but its effectiveness is limited by the need for extensive hyperparameter tuning. To address this issue, we propose a structure-aware PNN (SAPNN), which incorporates a NN layer to learn the structure of the product layer, thereby reducing the reliance on manual hyperparameter tuning. The SAPNN model is demonstrated to outperform the PNN model in terms of accuracy and efficiency on multiple real-world datasets.

This research focuses on the design of optimal beamforming techniques for intelligent reflecting surface-aided networks, where the transmitter has access to the intelligent reflecting surface, and aims to maximize the sum rate while minimizing the active transmit power. The challenge lies in the uncertainty of the channel state information, which necessitates a robust approach to ensure reliable performance. The problem is formulated as a robust optimization problem, which is then solved using a novel algorithm that combines the power cone and semidefinite relaxation techniques. The results show that the proposed method outperforms existing solutions in terms of sum rate and power consumption.

The conventional method of branch prediction, which relies on simple patterns, has been surpassed by deep learning-based dynamic predictors that analyze instruction sequences and generate prediction outcomes. However, the performance of these deep learning predictors is often compromised by the need for extensive training and the high computational costs involved. To address these limitations, we have developed a new branch prediction technique that leverages a lightweight neural network to make predictions based on previous branch outcomes. This approach is designed to be highly efficient, with a focus on minimizing the computational resources required for prediction. By employing a simple neural network that can be trained on a small dataset, our method achieves a high prediction accuracy while maintaining a low prediction overhead. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms existing branch prediction techniques, with a prediction accuracy of 99.9% and a prediction overhead of less than 10 cycles.

This study introduces a novel camera control system that leverages deep convolutional neural networks to achieve efficient target tracking and camera management. The proposed system, which is comprised of a CNN-based camera controller and a target monitoring network, is designed to optimize camera movement and focus. The target monitoring component utilizes a CNN architecture to identify and monitor targets, while the camera controller network determines the optimal camera position based on the target's location. The system's efficacy is demonstrated through a series of experiments on the UCF101 dataset, which reveal that the proposed approach outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency.

We have found a boundary law for the SOS model on a finite, possibly irregular, surface embedded within an infinite grid. This boundary law is not mathematically valid, yet it offers significant insights. It demonstrates that the probability distribution of the surface's geometry is directly proportional to a specific expression, comprising a product of geometric features and a boundary law. This boundary law is not normalizable, but it allows us to derive upper limits on the probabilities of specific geometric configurations. These limits are crucial in proving that the boundary of the surface exhibits a particular type of behavior, specifically the Kardar-Parisi-angasler type scaling, in dimensions greater than or equal to six.

We investigate the phenomenon of entangled two-photon resonance energy transfer (ETPR) from a donor to a receiver. This process is characterized by an effective rate coefficient, denoted as K_{E2P}, which is influenced by the properties of the donor and receiver, as well as the entanglement characteristics of the two-photon source. The two-photon resonance condition is met when the sum of the two-photon source frequency and the donor's transition frequency matches the receiver's transition frequency. Our research reveals that the efficiency of E2P is contingent upon the entanglement between the two photons and the inherent properties of the donor and receiver. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the E2P efficiency can be modulated by adjusting the two-photon source's frequency and the receiver's transition frequency. Our study also explores the potential of using E2P to investigate the entanglement between photons and the properties of the receiver.

The strong coupling constants of the $D_s^*$ and $D_s$ mesons are determined using the light-cone QCD sum rules approach, incorporating the light-cone distribution amplitudes of the $B_s$ meson. The coupling constants are calculated at the scale of the $D_s^*$ mass, utilizing the renormalization group to convert from the standard QCD scale. The results are compared to predictions made by the large-$N_c$ limit and the non-leptonic decay of the $B_s$ meson. The strong coupling constants are found to be in agreement with those predicted by the non-leptonic decay of the $B_s$ meson, but differ from those in the large-$N_c$ limit. The strong coupling constants are also used to predict the branching fractions of the non-leptonic decays of the $B_s$ meson, specifically $B_s \to D_s^* D_s \bar{K}$ and $B_s \to D_s D_s^* \bar{K}$. The predicted branching fractions are found to be in agreement with the experimental results.

Recent neutrino oscillation experiments at short and long baselines have revealed
anomalies that are currently being thoroughly examined. The short baseline
anomaly is particularly intriguing as it appears to be in line with the
sterile neutrino concept, yet it is contradicted by recent short-baseline
reactor experiments. The long baseline anomaly, on the other hand, is a
challenge to the three-neutrino model, especially considering the role of
non-unitary mixing. In this research, we explore the possibility of
simultaneously explaining both anomalies by incorporating a non-unitary
mixing matrix. The key to this lies in the introduction of new right-handed
neutrinos, which can be achieved through a specific type of mass matrix. The
non-unitary mixing matrix is then derived from this mass matrix, and we find
that it can provide a satisfactory explanation for both anomalies. The
implications of this research are significant, as it provides a potential
solution to the long-standing neutrino oscillation anomalies.

Researchers have been using linear regression to estimate the effect of a treatment on an outcome, but this approach can be inaccurate when the sample size is small or when there are many variables. To address this issue, we propose a new method that uses a Bayesian approach to adjust for covariates in observational studies. This approach involves using the posterior mean of the regression coefficients to weight the samples in the study, which can lead to more accurate estimates of the causal effect. We also show that our method can be used to identify important covariates in the study, which can help researchers design more effective observational studies. We also provide a method for calculating confidence intervals for the causal effect estimate, which can help researchers make more informed decisions about their studies. This research introduces a comprehensive analytical framework for determining the stability of a grid-connected voltage source converter (VSC) system, which incorporates a control strategy that combines active power and voltage regulation. The proposed model is based on a linearized small-signal analysis, which takes into account the dynamic behavior of the VSC and the power system. The model is validated through simulations of a 3-phase VSC connected to a weak grid, which demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed control strategy in maintaining stable operation. The results show that the proposed control strategy can effectively regulate the VSC's active power and voltage, even under varying load conditions. The model is also used to investigate the impact of the VSC's control parameters on the system's stability, which is found to be significant. The results of the simulations are compared with analytical predictions, which show good agreement. The proposed analytical framework is expected to provide a useful tool for understanding the stability of grid-connected VSC systems, which is critical for the development of renewable energy systems.

We've developed a method to measure the emitted light from an atomic ensemble using a single photon detector, allowing for the observation of quantum interference effects. Our approach relies on the principles of two-atom decay, where the light emitted from the ensemble shows quantum interference, resulting in a nonclassical photon source. By measuring the time difference between the emitted photons, we can demonstrate the entanglement between them, which can be verified through the observation of Hong-Ou-Mandel interference. Our experiment successfully generates entangled photons, as evidenced by the presence of a two-photon interference pattern with a visibility of 40%, and a corresponding Hong-Ou-Mandel dip with a visibility of 20%.

The stability of kinks in the Klein-Gordon and $\phi^4$ equations is examined, taking into account the influence of internal modes and the interaction between the kinks' translational mode and their internal modes. This analysis reveals that previous kink stability assessments were flawed, as they neglected the internal modes. By analyzing the squared eigenvalue spectrum, it is found that kinks are unstable for large coupling constants, with the magnitude of the unstable eigenvalues increasing as the internal modes' influence intensifies. This research also explores the kink's time-evolution under these unstable conditions, suggesting that the kink's stability is determined by the internal mode's energy, which can be either stabilizing or destabilizing depending on the kink's configuration.

The study of hadron production in high-energy hadron collisions can be described by generalized parton distributions (GPDs), which are typically associated with elastic scattering processes. This work examines how hadrons can be produced in elastic-like interactions, such as when a quark is ejected from a nucleon, resulting in the formation of a new hadron. The study focuses on the production of leading hadrons in high-energy collisions, which can be understood through the lens of factorized elastic-like interactions. The leading hadron's distribution is described by the nucleon's momentum-dependent parton distribution function, which is defined in terms of the nucleon's momentum space. The study also explores the implications of this understanding for the parton model, which is typically used to describe high-energy interactions.

Neural networks are often trained using a cross-entropy loss function, which can lead to overconfident predictions and poor generalization in real-world scenarios. To address this issue, we propose an enhanced cross-entropy loss function that incorporates discrete noise into the training process. By introducing discrete noise, the model learns a broader decision boundary, making it more robust to real-world data variations. We evaluated our approach on sentiment analysis and text classification tasks, and our results demonstrate its effectiveness in improving model generalization.

In endoscopic procedures, identifying polyps is crucial for preventing colorectal cancer.  Although deep learning has achieved notable success in this area, it still faces significant challenges due to the complexity of polyp detection.  To address this issue, we propose a novel channel-aware attention module that can be integrated into any existing network.  This module enhances the effectiveness of feature aggregation by assigning varying importance to different channels, thereby improving polyp detection accuracy.  To further enhance performance, we introduce a new training strategy that combines the advantages of both spatial and temporal features.  Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in polyp detection, achieving remarkable improvements in both the Kvasir-CLIP and CVC-Clinic-D datasets.

The samples are generated iteratively, where each new sample is drawn from the previous sample according to a Gaussian distribution, with the mean as the previous sample and the standard deviation as the standard deviation of the distribution. The process is accompanied by a proof of convergence, which demonstrates that the distribution of the samples converges to the target Gaussian density as the number of iterations approaches infinity. The method is also illustrated through numerical examples, which demonstrate its effectiveness in generating samples from distributions with varying levels of spreading.

contributed to our understanding of galactic sources of gamma-ray emission.

This research examines the impact of nonlocal boundary conditions on the diffusion process within a bounded area of n-dimensional space. The study's findings demonstrate that the influence of these boundary conditions is heavily influenced by the domain's geometric characteristics, particularly its size and shape. The study's results are supported by numerical simulations, which reveal that the influence of nonlocal boundary conditions can be significant and can lead to unexpected behavior in diffusion models.

Recommender Systems are complex systems that are difficult to analyze due to their intricate nature. To address this challenge, we propose a simulation-based approach that allows for the creation of virtual environments where the behavior of these systems can be studied. By leveraging simulation, we can gain insights into the underlying mechanisms of these systems and their impact on user experience. Our approach is demonstrated through a case study of a simulation of a mobile app store, where we analyze the effects of different simulation parameters on the simulation results. The results of this study show that simulation can be a valuable tool for understanding the behavior of complex systems and can contribute to the development of more effective recommender systems.

This paper examines the properties of truncated sample means, which are derived from samples from a distribution F, and their associated sample moments. Truncated moments are defined by the lower and upper bounds of the sample mean, specifically the minimum and maximum values in the sample. The paper establishes the asymptotic distribution of these sample means under various conditions, including when the mean of F is infinite or when it exists. Additionally, the consistency of these estimators is demonstrated. The results are then applied to the construction of hypothesis tests for distribution F, which can detect heavy-tailedness or finiteness of the mean or variance. The effectiveness of these tests is illustrated through simulations and a real-world application.

Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCI) utilize EEG data to develop systems that can control external devices through a person's thoughts.  A common approach to BCI involves using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to analyze EEG data, but their performance is often limited by the high dimensionality of the data and the limited availability of training samples.  To address these issues, we introduce a novel method that combines the strengths of CNNs and Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to improve BCI performance.  By applying a GNN to a graph representation of EEG data, we can effectively capture the spatial relationships between different brain regions, while a CNN extracts temporal features from the data.  Our approach leverages the complementary strengths of these two architectures to improve BCI performance, and we demonstrate its effectiveness on a large dataset of EEG recordings.

The application of $AdS/CFT$ correspondence to massive scalar fields in noncommutative spaces has been studied. A new approach to quantizing fields in noncommutative spaces has been introduced, which is based on the star product. This method has been used to calculate the scalar field's two-point function in AdS space, and it has been found that the result is equivalent to the thermal two-point function of a CFT in a noncommutative space.

The allocation of donated kidneys to patients in need is a critical process that significantly impacts the lives of thousands of individuals. In the United States, the United Network for Organ Transplantation (UNOS) oversees the allocation of these organs, employing a complex system that takes into account various factors such as patient condition, donor type, and transplant history. In this research, we introduce a Markov Decision Process (MDP) model that incorporates a patient's incompatibility status as a dynamic state variable, allowing for a more nuanced analysis of acceptance decisions. By doing so, we can better understand the trade-offs between immediate transplantation and preserving a patient's HLA type for future opportunities. Our model also considers the complexities of the UNOS system, including the allocation of different types of donated kidneys and the varying HLA match qualities. Through extensive simulations, we demonstrate that our model can effectively inform decision-making and optimize the overall allocation process.

This study compares the internal workings of Hidden Markov Models and Long Short-Term Memory Models, specifically focusing on their hidden state representations. We investigate how these states are organized in the context of HMMs and LSTMs, with a particular emphasis on understanding the underlying structure of the states in LSTMs. We introduce a new method for analyzing LSTM hidden states, which involves using a clustering technique to identify the most relevant states for each class. We then use a graph-based approach to determine the connectivity between these states and compare the results to HMM states. We also examine the impact of the learning algorithm on the structure of LSTMs by comparing the results of the clustering and graph-based approaches for different training methods. We find that the learning algorithm has a significant effect on the structure of the LSTMs, with the supervised training method producing more consistent results than the self-supervised training method. We also find that the learning algorithm can influence the connectivity between the states in LSTMs, with the supervised training method producing more consistent results than the self-supervised training method. We also investigate the relationship between the hidden states of HMMs and LSTMs, with a particular focus on the effect of the learning algorithm on the relationship between the hidden states of the two models. We find that the learning algorithm can influence the relationship between the hidden states of HMMs and LSTMs, with the supervised training method producing more consistent results than the self-supervised training method.
We determine the conditions under which certain operators involving fractional integrals are elements of the Schatten class on weighted Bergman spaces.

To address the challenge of deploying large language models on resource-constrained devices, we investigate the effectiveness of various compressed architectures in text classification tasks. We experiment with different compression techniques, including pruning, quantization, and knowledge distillation, and discover that the combination of these methods yields significant compression and performance improvements. We also find that the choice of architecture has a substantial impact on the results, and our experiments reveal that the best trade-off between compression and performance is achieved by using a specific architecture, which we refer to as the "CompressBERT" model. We demonstrate that our approach can achieve a compression ratio of up to 95% while maintaining performance within 5% of the original model, and our code is made available for public use.

This paper proposes the concept of a "Tooling" science to complement the existing framework of high energy physics, which comprises "Discovery" and "Understanding" sciences. The "Tooling" science would focus on developing advanced data analysis tools and software to facilitate the analysis of large datasets and the development of new tools for the field. It would also involve creating a diverse ecosystem of tools to support the various aspects of high energy physics research.
Building upon Richelot isogenies and generalized Howe curves, we examine decomposed compositions of these curves and the associated isogenies, providing a concrete example of the general phenomenon.

We've identified a group of magnetic hot subdwarfs with unique characteristics, including high hydrogen levels and a specific abundance of helium, which contrasts with the predictions of current stellar models. These magnetic hot subdwarfs were discovered through a combination of spectroscopic and photometric data, and their unusual properties suggest that they may have undergone a different evolutionary path than previously thought. In particular, the abundance of helium in these stars is significantly higher than predicted, and this discrepancy is thought to be the result of a unique process involving the diffusion of helium in the presence of a magnetic field. Our findings support the idea that magnetic hot subdwarfs may have a distinct evolutionary path, and that their unique properties can provide valuable insights into the behavior of magnetic fields in these stars.

This research focuses on the theoretical analysis of the error in matrices,
particularly in the context of deep learning. We investigate the properties of
errors in matrices that are invariant under certain transformations, and
demonstrate that the distribution of these invariant errors remains unchanged
when the transformation is applied. Furthermore, we establish that the
distribution of the Frobenius norm of the error is invariant under the same
conditions. We also derive a matrix representation of the error, which is
invariant under the transformation, and use this to develop a method for
measuring the error in matrices.

The Wikipedia link structure is a vital tool for understanding the encyclopedia's content, but its analysis is complicated by the fact that Wikipedia's internal data does not directly reflect the actual structure of its links. This is because the raw Wikipedia text contains a limited number of hyperlinks, whereas the HTML version includes a vast array of links, many of which are not relevant. To address this issue, we developed a filtering method to identify and remove irrelevant links, such as those in image captions and file descriptions. This method was tested on the English Wikipedia and found to be effective in reducing the number of irrelevant links, resulting in a more accurate representation of the encyclopedia's link structure. The results of our analysis show that the link structure of Wikipedia is more stable and less prone to change than previously thought, with only a small number of links being added or removed each year. This finding has significant implications for the study of Wikipedia's link structure, as it suggests that the raw wikitext and the filtered HTML version are more similar than previously thought.

The stacking of twisted bilayers offers a unique way to create new materials with complex properties.  By combining two-dimensional materials, researchers can create materials with unique electronic structures, which can be further modified by applying an electric field.  In this study, we explore the potential of applying an electric field to a bilayer of two-dimensional materials to create a new type of material with unique electronic properties.  By analyzing the electronic structure of twisted bilayers, we found that applying an electric field can induce a type of symmetry breaking that leads to the formation of a new type of material with unique electronic properties.  Theoretical models suggest that this effect can be used to create materials with unique electronic properties, such as materials with unique electronic properties that are not present in the individual layers.  The results of this study provide a new way to create materials with unique electronic properties, which can be used to develop new materials for a variety of applications.

We investigate the path of light in a non-flat universe with uniform expansion, revealing that its trajectory can be accurately represented by an equation similar to the one used for a flat universe, albeit with a modified parameter.

The movement of a liquid crystal suspended within a wavy wall containing hills and depressions was examined. The study found that the orientation of the liquid crystal, in combination with the wave pattern, influences the path of the colloid particles. The presence of a liquid crystal allows for the manipulation of the trajectory of the particles by adjusting the wave pattern and the liquid crystal's orientation.

A recent study by the OSIRIS-REx mission found that asteroid 101955 (Bennu) has a high elongation, which could be influenced by tidal forces beyond a certain distance. This study investigates the likelihood of this phenomenon by analyzing the shape of Bennu and its potential to break apart due to tidal forces. It is found that the asteroid's high elongation is unlikely to be caused by tidal forces, as Bennu's density is too low for this to be the case. Instead, the shape of Bennu is likely due to its initial formation process. This study also explores the relationship between an asteroid's elongation and its sensitivity to tidal forces, and finds that more elongated asteroids are more likely to break apart. It is suggested that tidal forces may have played a role in the formation of certain asteroids, such as 1991 BU, and that the shape of an asteroid can provide clues to its formation process.

The study of molecular dynamics simulations is crucial for understanding the behavior of molecules, but accurately capturing rare conformational transitions is a significant challenge. To address this issue, we propose an innovative approach that combines machine learning and quantum computing to identify and analyze these transitions. By utilizing machine learning techniques, we can identify key transition pathways, and then leverage quantum computing to calculate the associated free energy barriers. This approach has the potential to significantly advance our understanding of molecular dynamics simulations and open up new avenues for research in the field.

A newly developed Monte-Carlo code, MAPPIES, has been created to simulate the polarization of X-ray and gamma-ray emissions from astrophysical sources. MAPPIES takes into account the polarization effects of various processes, including Comptonization, inverse Compton scattering, and electron-positron pair production. The code's capabilities are demonstrated through its application to the polarization of cosmic gamma-ray background and X-ray emission from active galactic nuclei. MAPPIES's source code is freely available on GitHub at https://github.com/romainmarchand/MAPPies.

This research examines the impact of seasonal sea-ice thickness patterns on the Arctic's climate system, specifically focusing on the Arctic Ocean's seasonal cycle. By analyzing the Arctic's seasonal cycle, we investigate the role of sea-ice thickness categories in the climate system. To achieve this, we utilize a climate model, CESM, to simulate the Arctic's seasonal cycle, taking into account the effects of open water and sea-ice thickness categories. Our results show that the introduction of open water significantly alters the evolution of sea-ice thickness categories, leading to a more pronounced seasonal cycle. Furthermore, we find that the evolution of sea-ice thickness categories is influenced by the evolution of sea surface temperature, particularly in the Arctic's summer and fall seasons. Our findings suggest that the evolution of sea-ice thickness categories is closely linked to the evolution of sea surface temperature, particularly in the Arctic's summer and fall seasons.

This paper examines two distinct families of algebraic curves, denoted as $\mathcal{X}_{a,b,n,s}$ and $\mathcal{Y}_{n,s}$, which are defined over an algebraically closed field of characteristic $p$, where $p$ is greater than 2. The curve $\mathcal{X}_{a,b,n,s}$ is constructed from a specific type of Hermitian curve cover, while $\mathcal{Y}_{n,s}$ is a special case where $a=1$, $b=1$, and $n=s^2+1$. The study focuses on determining the Weierstrass semigroups of these curves, which in turn allows for the identification of their Weierstrass points. The research also yields specific examples of curves with high genus, along with their corresponding Weierstrass semigroups, and a set of non-Weierstrass pole orders at specified points.

Despite significant advancements in singing voice synthesis, it remains a complex and under-researched field, with applications in both commercial settings and academic pursuits.  However, a major challenge lies in the lack of a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating the quality of singing voice synthesis systems.  To address this issue, we introduce the 2021 ISMIR Singing Voice Synthesis Challenge, which aims to develop a standardized benchmark for assessing the quality of singing voice synthesis systems.  This benchmark will enable researchers to compare their results with those of other participants in a fair and objective manner.  To facilitate this, we have created a new dataset consisting of 1,000 high-quality singing audio recordings, which we have annotated with detailed phonetic and melodic information.  This dataset is available for public use, and we have also developed a baseline system that utilizes a pre-trained neural network to generate singing audio from a given input.  This baseline system serves as a starting point for researchers who wish to explore the field of singing voice synthesis.  In addition to the dataset and baseline system, we have also provided a set of evaluation metrics that can be used to assess the quality of singing voice synthesis systems.  These metrics include both objective and subjective measures, which are designed to provide a comprehensive evaluation of the quality of singing voice synthesis systems.  Overall, the ISMIR Singing Voice Synthesis Challenge aims to advance the field of singing voice synthesis by providing a standardized benchmark for assessing the quality

Ecoacoustic research has seen significant growth in recent years, with applications in monitoring bird populations, tracking forest health, and detecting invasive species.  A new tool, NIPS4Bplus, has been developed to assist researchers in analyzing the sounds of bird populations.  This software allows users to automatically identify bird calls and estimate the number of birds in a given area.  By using a combination of advanced machine learning techniques, NIPS4Bplus can accurately identify bird calls and estimate the number of birds in a given area.  This tool has been tested on a dataset of bird calls from a specific region, and the results show that it can accurately identify bird calls and estimate the number of birds in a given area.  NIPS4Bplus is a powerful tool that can be used to improve our understanding of bird populations and their habitats.

This research presents a calibration framework for event and frame-based sensors, enabling accurate calibration of both eye and image sensors, as well as determining the relative position and orientation between the two types of sensors. The proposed method leverages a monocular video frame and an event stream captured simultaneously, utilizing a straightforward and efficient approach. The framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through its successful application to diverse eye and event camera setups, including scenarios where the sensors are positioned at different distances and angles. The framework's performance is evaluated using both synthetic and real-world datasets, showcasing its robustness and accuracy.

Graph learning has proven to be effective in numerous fields, including social media, e-commerce, and knowledge graphs, but its applications are not limited to these areas. This research paper highlights the potential of graph learning in various other domains, including natural language processing, computer vision, and bioinformatics. We also discuss the potential of graph learning in addressing complex challenges in science and engineering, such as protein design, autonomous driving, and robotics.

We establish a link between the braid group acting on a specific set of objects in a mathematical space and a related geometric structure, which in turn corresponds to a well-known geometric arrangement.

A new technique for 3D navigation in retinal surgery has been developed, utilizing a spotlight projection system. This approach involves projecting a 3D pattern onto the retina to provide real-time guidance to the surgeon. A projection model is created by analyzing the optical properties of the eye, allowing for accurate calculation of the projection's appearance on the retina. A specialized camera captures the projected pattern, and a neural network analyzes the captured images to determine the 3D position and orientation of the eye. The network is trained using a large dataset of simulated images, and it can accurately predict the eye's pose in real-time. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this technique, achieving high accuracy in 3D navigation. This technology has the potential to revolutionize retinal surgery by providing surgeons with a more precise and efficient way to navigate the eye.

This paper presents a novel product formula for $F$-polynomials in the context of mutation-flip equivalence, which can be expressed as an infinite sum. By employing this product formula, we derive a specific instance of the $F$-polynomials corresponding to the cluster algebra associated with the $D_4$ quiver, which is a mutation-flip equivalence class.

The FIDO2 standard has accelerated the shift towards passwordless authentication, but its widespread adoption is hindered by the requirement for a compatible authentication server. This server can be supplied by the identity provider or the service provider, but the latter is more common. This paper examines the challenges and opportunities for service providers in implementing a passwordless authentication system using FIDO2. It also presents a FIDO2-based passwordless authentication system for the University of Pretoria's web portal, which has been successfully tested.

A novel approach to the Weyl-Wigner formalism has been developed to address the quantum mechanics of qubits, but it fails to capture the essence of quantum physics. This new framework neglects the inherent non-commutative properties of quantum states, rendering them indistinguishable from classical statistical mixtures. As a result, it overlooks the unique characteristics of quantum systems, such as quantum interference and the Heisenberg uncertainty principle. This new method also treats all quantum states as equivalent, disregarding the distinction between pure and mixed states.

This research paper examines how users can control their experience when watching videos, with a focus on the importance of user control in human-computer interaction. It explores various user interface elements in video apps, such as playback controls and interactive elements, that enable users to customize their experience. The paper also discusses the potential of interactive elements like video games and interactive storytelling to enhance user control. Furthermore, it discusses the impact of user control on video streaming services and presents a classification of video apps based on their primary function. The paper concludes by highlighting the potential of user-controlled video apps to create engaging and interactive experiences, and suggests future research directions in this area.

This new approach draws inspiration from the Gray codes of Binet-Euler, specifically designed for Catalan numbers, and incorporates a straightforward algorithm for node insertion and deletion based on the binomial trees' recursive properties.

Reconstructing tracks in heavy ion collision events is a complex process due to the numerous particles produced during the collision. This study presents a novel approach to track reconstruction, utilizing a graph neural network to identify and classify tracks. The proposed method was tested using simulated data from the LHCb detector and demonstrated to be effective in tracking particles with high momentum and low mass. The results show that the neural network approach achieves high accuracy in tracking particles, even in the presence of high background noise. The study also explores the potential of the method to be applied to real-world data and other experiments.

The proposed method, which combines free-surface flow dynamics with the space-time analysis of prismatic elements, is thoroughly examined and validated through a series of rigorous tests, including simulations of free-surface flows in a two-dimensional channel, a rectangular tank, and a two-dimensional dam break scenario.
